newsitem.title: USA: Construction spending unexpectedly strong in September.
newsitem.headline: Construction spending unexpectedly strong in September.

text.p: Construction spending rose unexpectedly in September, boosted by the biggest jump in government-financed building projects in more than 5-1/2 years, the Commerce Department said Monday.

Total spending on new construction rose 1.9 percent to a record annual rate of $573.4 billion in September, the department said. It was the biggest increase since a 2.3 percent gain in March and stood in contrast to private economists' forecasts of a 0.1 percent decline.
Analysts said stronger government spending was taking up the slack from sluggish private-sector spending after a strong first half in which new housing construction surged.

Spending on privately financed and public projects rose in September, but by far the largest part of the increase came in government spending, which jumped 6.4 percent to a $147 billion rate after falling 1.4 percent in August.
There were big gains in spending to improve highways and streets and smaller increases for housing and redevelopment, schools and hospitals and for water treatment plants.
Spending edged up 0.4 percent to $426.4 billion on private projects after rising 1.4 percent in August.

"The data ... indicate that private construction outlays remain weak and that pubic outlays are essentially supporting the construction industry," said Marilyn Schaja, economist for Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp. in New York.
The department said spending on construction of single-family homes fell to $155.9 billion in September from $157.3 billion in August.
"Residential construction spending is slipping, but not by very much," said economist Cynthia Latta of DRI/McGraw Hill Inc. in Lexington, Mass.
The department said last month that construction starts on new homes and apartments fell 6 percent in September after a 4 percent August gain.
Latta noted there were signs that office-building could pick up since shortages of space in many cities were pushing commercial rents higher.
"I think we can look forward to some recovery on the commercial side over the next year," Latta said.
During September, spending on new non-residential buildings like offices and industrial parks jumped to a $142.3 billion rate from $140.3 billion in August.

After allowing for inflation, total construction spending rose 1.7 percent in September to a seasonally adjusted $496.3 billion annual rate following a 0.5 percent rise in August, the department said.
